breakfast.name: Mate
ingredients: Yerba mate (dried leaves and stems of Ilex paraguariensis)
Bombilla (metal straw with a filter at the bottom)
instructions: Mate is not just a drink in Uruguay -- it is the national identity
Uruguay has the highest per-capita mate consumption in the world -- higher than Argentina or Paraguay
Carried everywhere: Uruguayans walk with a thermos under one arm and a mate gourd in hand
The water must be hot but NOT boiling -- boiling water burns the yerba and makes it bitter
Drunk continuously throughout the day -- it is a constant companion, not a single serving
In social settings, one person (the cebador) prepares and passes the mate around the circle
Each person drinks the full gourd through the bombilla and returns it for refilling
Sharing mate is an act of friendship and trust
breakfast.description: Uruguayan national identity drink -- yerba mate (Ilex paraguariensis) steeped in a gourd with a bombilla (filtered metal straw). Hot water, never boiling (burns the yerba). Carried everywhere with a thermos. Uruguay has the world's highest per-capita consumption. Shared in a circle: the cebador prepares, each person drinks and returns.

breakfast.name: Bizcocho (Flaky Pastries)
instructions: Bizcochos are the Uruguayan pastry eaten with mate
A flaky, buttery pastry -- like a cross between a croissant and puff pastry
The savory version: flaky, salty, made with beef fat (grasa)
The sweet version: dusted with sugar
Bought at the panaderia (bakery) every morning
Bizcochos with mate: the Uruguayan morning ritual
breakfast.description: Uruguayan flaky pastries -- bizcochos, puff-pastry-like, made with butter or beef fat (grasa). Savory (salty) or sweet (sugared). Bought at the panaderia every morning. Eaten with mate: the Uruguayan morning ritual.

breakfast.name: Tortas Fritas (Fried Bread on Rainy Days)
instructions: Tortas fritas are the Uruguayan fried bread -- but only made on rainy days
The tradition: when it rains, you make tortas fritas -- the association is deeply ingrained
Simple fried dough -- flattened discs fried until puffed and golden
Dusted with sugar
Eaten with mate
The rainy day tradition is taken seriously -- asking for tortas fritas on a sunny day is odd
breakfast.description: Uruguayan rainy-day fried bread -- tortas fritas, simple dough discs fried until puffed and golden, dusted with sugar. The tradition: tortas fritas are made ONLY on rainy days. The association is deeply ingrained in Uruguayan culture. Eaten with mate.

breakfast.name: Medialunas (Croissants)
ingredients: Flour, yeast, butter, eggs, sugar, milk
instructions: Medialunas are Uruguayan croissants -- half moons
Two types: de manteca (buttery, croissant-like) and de grasa (made with beef fat, savory)
Smaller than French croissants
Glazed with simple syrup after baking -- shiny and slightly sticky
Eaten at cafes with coffee or mate
The Rioplatense cafe culture (shared with Buenos Aires) centers on medialunas and cafe con leche
breakfast.description: Uruguayan half-moon croissants -- medialunas, smaller than French, two types: de manteca (buttery) and de grasa (beef fat, savory). Glazed with simple syrup after baking. The Rioplatense cafe culture centers on medialunas and cafe con leche.

lunch.name: Asado (Grilled Beef)
ingredients: Beef: tira de asado (cross-cut short ribs), vacio (flank), entrana (skirt steak), chorizo (sausage), morcilla (blood sausage)
Wood or charcoal (lena -- wood is preferred for flavor)
Chimichurri (parsley, garlic, oregano, red pepper, olive oil, vinegar)
instructions: Asado is the Uruguayan (and Argentine) ritual of grilled beef
Uruguay has more cattle per capita than almost any country on earth
The asado is not just cooking -- it is a social event, an afternoon-long ritual
The asador (the person who grills) controls the fire, the timing, and the order of meats
The parrilla (grill) uses wood or charcoal -- gas is unacceptable for asado purists
The meat is seasoned only with coarse salt -- nothing else
The order: chorizos and morcilla first (appetizer), then the beef cuts
Chimichurri on the side -- the Argentine-Uruguayan herb sauce
The asado is the Sunday family gathering -- every week, rain or shine
lunch.description: Uruguayan grilled beef ritual -- asado, an afternoon-long social event. Beef seasoned only with coarse salt, grilled over wood on a parrilla. Chorizos and morcilla first, then beef cuts (tira de asado, vacio, entrana). Chimichurri on the side. Uruguay has more cattle per capita than almost any country. The Sunday family gathering.

lunch.name: Chivito (Steak Sandwich)
ingredients: Bread roll (a firm roll that can hold the weight)
instructions: The chivito is Uruguay's national sandwich -- and it is enormous
A thin steak with ham, bacon, mozzarella, fried egg, lettuce, tomato, olives, and mayo
All stacked in a bread roll -- the roll must be firm enough to hold everything
Invented in Punta del Este in the 1940s -- a customer asked for goat (chivito) but the restaurant didn't have any, so they improvised with steak
Named chivito (little goat) even though it has never contained goat
Served with fries on the side
The Uruguayan answer to a burger -- but much more loaded
lunch.description: Uruguayan national steak sandwich -- chivito, a thin beef steak with ham, bacon, mozzarella, fried egg, lettuce, tomato, olives, and mayo in a firm roll. Named "little goat" though it never contained goat (invented when a restaurant ran out of goat). Invented in Punta del Este, 1940s. Served with fries.

lunch.name: Empanadas
ingredients: Filling: ground beef (carne) with onion, bell pepper, cumin, paprika, olives, hard-boiled egg
Or: ham and cheese, or spinach and cheese
instructions: Uruguayan empanadas are baked (not fried like Argentine empanadas, usually)
The meat filling: ground beef with onion, cumin, olives, and hard-boiled egg
The repulgue (edge crimp): each region and each cook has their own style
Eaten as a lunch, snack, or appetizer before asado
Sold at every bakery and supermarket
lunch.description: Uruguayan baked meat pastries -- empanadas, ground beef with onion, cumin, olives, and hard-boiled egg in a flour pastry. The repulgue (edge crimp) is each cook's signature. Typically baked (not fried). Eaten before asado or as a quick lunch.

lunch.name: Milanesa (Breaded Cutlet)
ingredients: Milanesa a la napolitana: tomato sauce, ham, and mozzarella melted on top
instructions: Milanesa is the Rioplatense breaded cutlet -- from the Italian Milanese tradition
Italian immigrants brought the cotoletta alla milanese to the River Plate
Pounded thin, breaded, and fried in oil
Eaten with lemon squeezed on top
Milanesa a la napolitana: with tomato sauce, ham, and melted cheese on top -- a hybrid
Milanesa a caballo: with fried eggs on top (a caballo = on horseback)
Every Uruguayan eats milanesa weekly -- it is the everyday comfort food
lunch.description: Uruguayan breaded cutlet -- milanesa, thin beef or chicken pounded, breaded, and fried (Italian Milanese heritage via River Plate immigration). Eaten with lemon. Milanesa a la napolitana: topped with tomato sauce, ham, and melted mozzarella. Every Uruguayan eats milanesa weekly.

lunch.name: Guiso de Lentejas (Lentil Stew)
instructions: Guiso de lentejas is the Uruguayan homestyle lentil stew
A hearty one-pot stew with lentils, vegetables, and chorizo
The chorizo colorado (red-cured sausage) gives it a smoky-spiced depth
A winter comfort food
Spanish and Italian immigrant influence on Rioplatense home cooking
lunch.description: Uruguayan hearty lentil stew -- lentils with chorizo colorado (cured red sausage for smoky depth), potato, carrot, and tomato. A winter comfort food. Spanish and Italian immigrant influence on Rioplatense home cooking.

dinner.name: Parrillada (Mixed Grill Platter)
ingredients: Beef cuts: entrana, asado, colita de cuadril
Morcilla (blood sausage with rice or onion filling)
instructions: A parrillada is the mixed grill served at Uruguayan parrilla restaurants
Unlike home asado (which is a slow ritual), restaurant parrillada is a curated platter
Includes a selection of beef cuts, offal (sweetbreads, kidneys), sausages, and provoleta
Provoleta: a disc of provolone cheese grilled directly on the parrilla until bubbly and charred underneath
Sweetbreads (molleja): prized in River Plate cuisine -- crispy outside, creamy inside
The Rioplatense tradition of eating all parts of the animal -- nose to tail
dinner.description: Uruguayan mixed grill platter -- curated selection of beef cuts, fresh chorizo, morcilla (blood sausage), molleja (sweetbreads: crispy outside, creamy inside), and provoleta (provolone grilled on the parrilla until bubbly). The Rioplatense nose-to-tail tradition. Served at parrilla restaurants.

dinner.name: Pascualina (Spinach and Egg Pie)
ingredients: Puff pastry or filo (for the shell and lid)
Hard-boiled eggs (whole, embedded in the filling)
instructions: Pascualina is the Uruguayan spinach pie -- Italian heritage (torta pasqualina from Genoa)
A deep pie with spinach and ricotta, whole hard-boiled eggs nested inside
When sliced, each slice reveals a cross-section of the embedded egg
Traditionally made at Easter (Pasqua = Easter in Italian)
Genoese immigrants (many came to the River Plate) brought the tradition
Now eaten year-round as a main course or lunch
dinner.description: Uruguayan Italian-heritage spinach pie -- pascualina, puff pastry shell filled with spinach and ricotta, whole hard-boiled eggs embedded (cross-section visible when sliced). From Genoese torta pasqualina (Easter tradition). Genoese immigrants brought it to the River Plate. Now year-round.

dinner.name: Buseca (Tripe Stew)
instructions: Buseca is the Uruguayan tripe stew -- Italian heritage (busecca from Milan)
Tripe slow-cooked with white beans, chorizo, and vegetables
A rich, hearty winter stew
Eaten at home on cold nights
The Milanese Italian community brought the tradition
dinner.description: Uruguayan Italian-heritage tripe stew -- buseca, tripe slow-cooked with white beans, chorizo colorado, and vegetables. From Milanese busecca. Rich and hearty, eaten on cold winter nights.

dinner.name: Tallarines con Tuco (Pasta with Meat Sauce)
ingredients: Tuco: ground beef, onion, garlic, carrot, tomato passata
instructions: Tallarines con tuco is the Rioplatense pasta with meat sauce -- Italian immigrant food
Tuco is the Rioplatense word for a slow-cooked meat and tomato sauce
From the Italian sugo/tuco
Italian immigration to Uruguay was massive -- shaping the cuisine fundamentally
Between 1860-1920, hundreds of thousands of Italians (mostly from Genoa, Calabria, Naples) settled in Montevideo
This is everyday home cooking -- not fancy, but foundational
dinner.description: Uruguayan Italian-heritage pasta -- tallarines (flat noodles) with tuco (slow-cooked meat and tomato sauce, from Italian sugo). Generous parmesan. Italian immigration (1860-1920, mainly Genoese, Calabrian, Neapolitan) fundamentally shaped Uruguayan cuisine. This is everyday home cooking.

dinner.name: Faina (Chickpea Flatbread)
instructions: Faina is the Uruguayan chickpea flatbread -- from Italian farinata (Genoa)
A simple batter of chickpea flour, water, and olive oil, baked in a very hot oven
Thin, slightly crispy on top, creamy inside
In Uruguay: faina is eaten ON TOP of pizza -- a slice of faina placed on a slice of pizza
The pizza-faina combination is uniquely Rioplatense -- nowhere else combines them
Sold at every pizzeria in Montevideo
dinner.description: Uruguayan chickpea flatbread -- faina (from Genoese farinata), chickpea flour baked thin and crispy. In Uruguay: eaten ON TOP of pizza -- a slice of faina placed on a pizza slice. The pizza-faina combination is uniquely Rioplatense. Sold at every Montevideo pizzeria.

snacks.name: Alfajor
ingredients: Dulce de leche (thick caramelized milk filling)
instructions: Alfajores are the River Plate cookie sandwich -- dulce de leche between two soft cookies
Dulce de leche: milk and sugar cooked slowly until caramelized -- the Rioplatense sweet staple
Alfajor brands (Portezuelo in Uruguay) are national pride
Chocolate-coated or dusted in powdered sugar or coconut
Eaten as a snack, dessert, or with mate and coffee
The alfajor came from Spain (Arab origin al-hasu) and was adapted in South America
snacks.description: Uruguayan dulce de leche sandwich cookies -- alfajores, two soft shortbread cookies with dulce de leche (slow-caramelized milk) between, coated in chocolate or powdered sugar. From Spanish (Arab origin al-hasu), adapted in South America. Portezuelo is the Uruguayan brand. National snack.

snacks.name: Chorizo al Pan (Choripan)
ingredients: Chimichurri or salsa criolla (tomato, onion, pepper, vinegar)
instructions: Choripan is the River Plate grilled sausage sandwich
A fresh chorizo grilled on the parrilla, placed in a crusty roll
Chimichurri or salsa criolla on top
The appetizer before asado -- or a stand-alone street food
Sold at football (soccer) matches, street fairs, and every parrilla
snacks.description: Uruguayan grilled sausage sandwich -- choripan, fresh chorizo grilled on the parrilla, placed in a crusty roll with chimichurri. The appetizer before asado. Sold at football matches, street fairs, and every parrilla.

snacks.name: Tarta de Jamon y Queso (Ham and Cheese Tart)
instructions: Tarta de jamon y queso is the everyday Uruguayan savory tart
Ham and cheese in a pastry shell with an egg custard poured over
Baked until golden
Eaten for lunch, dinner, or packed for school and work lunches
The Uruguayan answer to a quiche
snacks.description: Uruguayan everyday savory tart -- ham, cheese, and egg custard in a pastry shell. The Uruguayan quiche, eaten for lunch or packed for school and work.

snacks.name: Martin Fierro (Cheese and Quince Paste)
ingredients: Queso (semi-hard cheese -- like gouda or provolone)
Dulce de membrillo (quince paste -- firm, dark, sweet-tart)
instructions: Martin Fierro is the Uruguayan and Argentine pairing of cheese and quince paste
Named after the epic gaucho poem Martin Fierro by Jose Hernandez (1872)
A slice of cheese placed on a slice of quince paste
Sweet-savory-tart: the combination is addictive
Served as a snack, appetizer, or after-meal palate cleanser
The gaucho tradition: simple, protein-and-sugar, eaten on the pampa
snacks.description: Uruguayan cheese and quince paste pairing -- Martin Fierro, named after the gaucho epic poem (1872). A slice of semi-hard cheese with a slice of dulce de membrillo (quince paste). Sweet-savory-tart. The gaucho tradition: simple food of the pampa.

desserts.name: Dulce de Leche
instructions: Dulce de leche is the Rioplatense caramelized milk -- Uruguay and Argentina both claim it
Milk and sugar cooked very slowly for 1-2 hours, stirring constantly
The Maillard reaction: the milk proteins and sugar caramelize to a deep amber color
The result: thick, spreadable, intensely sweet caramel
Used in everything: alfajores, pancakes, toast, ice cream, cakes
The claim wars between Uruguay and Argentina over who invented it are intense
The global spread: dulce de leche is now available worldwide, but the Rioplatense version is the standard
desserts.description: Rioplatense caramelized milk -- dulce de leche, whole milk and sugar slow-cooked for 1-2 hours until Maillard-browned to deep amber. Thick, spreadable, intensely sweet. Used in everything. Uruguay and Argentina both claim the invention. The Rioplatense version is the global standard.

desserts.name: Chaja (Sponge Cake with Meringue and Peaches)
instructions: Chaja is the signature Uruguayan cake -- from the city of Paysandu
Invented by confectioner Orlando Castellano in 1927
Named after the chaja bird (screamer bird) native to Uruguay -- the meringue resembles its fluffy plumage
Layers of sponge cake, dulce de leche, whipped cream, crushed meringue, and peaches
Light, airy, and indulgent
The original is from Confiteria Las Familias in Paysandu
desserts.description: Uruguayan signature cake from Paysandu -- chaja, sponge cake layered with dulce de leche, whipped cream, crushed meringue, and peaches. Invented 1927 by Orlando Castellano. Named for the chaja bird (screamer bird): the meringue resembles its fluffy plumage. Light and indulgent.

desserts.name: Postre Chaja (Variation) -- Flan con Dulce de Leche
ingredients: Sugar (for the flan and for the caramel)
instructions: Flan con dulce de leche is the ubiquitous Rioplatense dessert
A baked custard (flan) with a caramel base
The addition of dulce de leche drizzled over the top is the Rioplatense twist
Sometimes whipped cream as well
Served at every restaurant in Uruguay
The combination of caramel (from the flan mold), custard, and dulce de leche is triple-caramel
desserts.description: Uruguayan triple-caramel custard -- flan (baked egg custard with caramel base), topped with dulce de leche drizzle. The caramel from the mold + the custard + the dulce de leche = three layers of caramel sweetness. Served at every Uruguayan restaurant.

drinks.name: Mate (Served Throughout the Day)
instructions: This entry is for mate as an all-day drink -- not just breakfast
Uruguayans drink mate continuously throughout the day
Walking, working, at the beach, in meetings
The thermos under the arm is the universal Uruguayan image
More than a drink: a social bond, a ritual, an identity marker
drinks.description: Uruguayan all-day ritual -- mate is not a single serving but a continuous companion. Carried everywhere with a thermos. Walking, working, at the beach, in meetings. More than a drink: a social bond, a ritual, an identity marker. The thermos under the arm is the universal Uruguayan image.

drinks.name: Medio y Medio (Half and Half)
ingredients: Sparkling sweet white wine or moscato (half)
instructions: Medio y medio is the Uruguayan cocktail from Montevideo's Ciudad Vieja
Half dry sparkling wine, half sweet sparkling wine -- combined
Associated with Cafe Roldos (Mercado del Puerto, Montevideo)
Drunk at the Mercado del Puerto while eating a parrillada
A Montevideo tradition -- not found elsewhere
drinks.description: Montevideo cocktail -- medio y medio (half and half), dry and sweet sparkling wine combined. Associated with Cafe Roldos at the Mercado del Puerto. Drunk while eating parrillada. A Montevideo tradition.

drinks.name: Grappamiel (Grappa with Honey)
ingredients: Grappa (Italian-style grape pomace spirit -- distilled in Uruguay)
instructions: Grappamiel is the Uruguayan honey-infused grappa
Grappa: the Italian grape pomace spirit, produced in Uruguay by Italian immigrant descendants
Mixed with honey -- the sweetness softens the grappa burn
Drunk as a digestif or warming winter drink
The Italian immigrant influence in Uruguayan spirits
drinks.description: Uruguayan honey grappa -- grappamiel, Italian-heritage grape pomace spirit (grappa) mixed with honey. The honey softens the burn. Drunk as a digestif or winter warmer. Italian immigrant distilling tradition preserved in Uruguay.
